title: The Weight of Survival
author: William Saville
content:
Wesley adjusted his wheelchair in front of the TV, the urgent broadcast blaring across the room. Agate stood nearby, wringing their hands, anxiety evident in their stance. On the screen, the somber face of an international official filled the frame.

“To ensure humanity’s survival,” the announcer declared, “the elite, those responsible for the depletion of Earth’s resources, have been flagged. Their DNA is banned from boarding evacuation ships. This decision ensures resources are shared fairly, and the mistakes of the past do not follow us into the stars.”

Wesley felt a strange sense of justice stir within him. For years, the wealthy had hoarded resources, leaving others to suffer. Now, the tables were turning. The neglected and forgotten (the disabled and the veterans) were being prioritized to ensure they wouldn’t be left behind. They were given “green” status. Wesley glanced at Agate, who nodded silently. In the background, their cats Calypso and Hollie watched the chaos on the streets below from the windowsill. Oswald, Wesley’s service cat, sat calmly in his lap, the little angel wings on his harness stark against the turmoil outside.

“We should go,” Agate said, voice trembling. “They’ll be opening the gates soon.”

Wesley patted Oswald’s head, grounding himself with the cat’s steady purring. “Alright,” he replied. “Let’s get packed.”

The streets outside were chaotic. People ran with bags, crates, and even animals in tow. Sirens wailed in the distance. Wesley and Agate maneuvered carefully, Wesley’s wheelchair loaded with carriers for Calypso and Hollie. Oswald remained on Wesley’s lap, ever watchful for signs of seizures or narcolepsy. As they approached the shipyard, the sounds of goats and pigs echoed from a nearby loading area. Farmers, priority evacuees, ushered their animals into designated sections.

At the gates, tension was thick. A man in an expensive suit argued with security, waving a gold wristwatch as a bribe. “I can pay anything you want,” he pleaded. The guard remained impassive. “Your DNA is flagged. Step aside.” The man’s desperate shouts faded as he was escorted away, a reminder of the new order.

Wesley and Agate presented their identification. Wesley drove through the scanner with Oswald. The scanner blinked green, and the guard smiled. “Welcome aboard.” Next was Agate, whose purple ID (reserved for caregivers) was accepted. Inside, the ship was a marvel of engineering. Their cabin was near the exits, as all disabled cabins were placed closest to the community areas for convenience. It was small, but bigger than the apartment they’d once shared. The cabin boasted state-of-the-art accessibility features: lowered counters, a fully stocked kitchenette that Wesley could use by driving up under the counter, grab bars, and an emergency intercom system. A screen on the wall offered meal delivery options for those unable to make it to the mess hall or cook due to pain.

“They thought of everything,” Agate said, their voice soft with relief. Wesley nodded, adjusting Oswald’s harness. The cat, ever vigilant, rubbed his head against Wesley’s hand before resuming his watchful stance. “This might actually work,” Wesley said, hope flickering in his voice.

The community areas buzzed with life. Families, scientists, and farmers mingled, each group bringing their own energy. Wesley wheeled through the crowd, Oswald drawing smiles and waves. “Look at his little wings!” a child exclaimed. People young and old flocked to Oswald to pet him and adore him, but ever the vigilant kitty, he remained in work mode, checking on Wesley but enjoying the attention, as he usually did when accompanying Wesley to medical appointments and errands.

Agate, however, grew visibly tense. The noise and movement were overwhelming. “I need to step away,” they whispered, giving Wesley a quick kiss before retreating to their quarters. Wesley understood. He stayed, letting Oswald’s calm presence anchor him. Though overstimulated by the noise and chaos, he felt grounded with Oswald on his lap, as the eyes in the room never seemed to focus on him in his wheelchair, only on Oswald.

One woman, a retired doctor, shared stories of her work in war zones with Doctors Without Borders. A farmer described plans for the onboard greenhouses, where pigs and goats would be raised alongside crops to provide rich fertilizer. A young boy with disheveled black hair proudly displayed his family’s heirloom seeds. Students of law, medicine, programming, and more found common ground, collaborating to create programs for their new society. A history professor and a language professor worked with an older programmer to build archives of Earth’s language, history, and culture. A lone violinist played, joined by other musicians, while a veteran with a prosthetic leg tapped his foot to the rhythm, his prosthesis resting on his lap for a break. An eccentric barber sporting a rainbow flag as a belt gave a much-needed haircut to a laughing teenager with a lip ring. Each story added a layer to the patchwork of humanity aboard the ship.

Back in their cabin, Wesley and Agate unpacked. Calypso and Hollie cautiously explored, sniffing every corner, joined by Oswald once his harness was off, signifying he was “off duty” and could be a regular cat. Wesley’s gaze lingered on the screen. “We should sign up for meal deliveries,” he suggested. “Just in case.”

Agate nodded, their shoulders relaxing. “Good idea.”

As the ship prepared for launch, another announcement echoed over the intercom: “We leave behind a world ravaged by greed. Together, we will build a future rooted in equity and compassion. Thank you for being part of this journey.”

Wesley reached for Agate’s hand. “We made it,” he said. Agate squeezed his hand tightly. “We did.”

The launch was a surreal experience. The vibration of the engines, the weightlessness as they broke free from Earth’s gravity, it was both exhilarating and sobering. Through the small cabin window, Wesley watched the planet shrink into the distance. “Goodbye, Earth,” he whispered. “Let’s do better this time.”

Over the following days, life aboard the ship settled into a routine. Wesley and Agate balanced time in the community areas with quiet moments in their cabin. Oswald continued to bring joy to everyone, his winged harness becoming a symbol of hope. People wondered if he liked being a service animal, and Wesley would tell them how Oswald would scream at the door and refuse to take care of his own needs when Wesley was out of the house for hours or days, depending on the medical need. By bringing Oswald with him, he was taking care of Oswald too, because the cat would only take care of himself if he knew Wesley was okay. He’d trained himself to alert for seizures and narcolepsy, making Wesley a very lucky guy. The conversations often shifted to miracle cats, with people discussing their own past feline companions and how cats were underappreciated in favor of dogs and miniature horses as service animals, despite their immense worth. Children would often stop by their cabin just to see Oswald, his face appearing on the outer door screen for the “doorbell” and sniffing the cabin camera while Agate held him up to greet them. The kids would run away laughing, their joy filling the sterile hallways.

One evening, Wesley and Agate sat together, watching a live broadcast from Earth. It showed the chaos left behind: the elites scrambling, their power meaningless.

“Justice,” Agate murmured.

Wesley nodded, but his heart ached for those who hadn’t made it. The weight of survival was heavy, but so was the promise of a fresh start.

“We have a chance to do this right,” Wesley said. Agate leaned their head on his shoulder. “Let’s make it count.”
